comments.author: rcr-anti
comments.text: While still possible, the proof exploiting a bug is vanishingly small now. Following a few bugs and bad proofs this year, there are a number of different implementations, in different languages, and with different levels of proofs of their consistency. con-leche and con-ron are the heavy hitters, with consistency proofs of themselves. So for RH to be false, there'd have to be a bug in all the kernels that affects both the consistency proofs and the RH proof itself.

comments.author: thejokeisonme
comments.text: A fake refutation of the Collatz conjecture already got through one of these independent checkers in the past. What's harder, proving GRH or finding a way to get through every checker (which aren't as independent as they are sometimes touted to be)? In this case there was a human expert in the loop so it's much less likely the model hacked its way through the problem without the expert noticing. But the statement as written has 4 points, none of which rests on the human involvement. So I don't like that they claim full confidence based on those points.

comments.author: senko
comments.text: This reminds me of a (completely different, but felt equally) bizzare problem with ghostty (the terminal emulator) on Linux and Steam, specifically Baldur's Gate 3. At the start of the game after an update, BG3 compiles the (Vulkan) shaders. To avoid hammering the computer, it checks the load, including I/O pressure, and then throttles itself. It turns out that Ghostty uses io_uring, and even if it's not doing anything this somehow counts as pressure. This was made worse by the fact that I usually have a dozen or so Ghostty windows. End result, BG3 compiles shaders using 1 core, throttled, instead of all available 20 cores. Instead of a minute or so, it'd take several hours. (For closure: I configured ghostty to use epoll instead. Probably not optimal but works around the problem.)

comments.author: manarth
comments.text: Better description: "My USB network switch was cutting my download speed". The fact that it's a monitor is a little bit irrelevant.

comments.author: fancyfredbot
comments.text: Since lots of comments misunderstood the article, the extra latency from going through the monitor meant his laptop couldn't acknowledge the packets quickly enough. That led a buffer on the ethernet adapter to fill and that led it to drop packets. A different adapter which required less frequent acknowledgement fixed the problem for him. It is quite a nice post which gets to the bottom of incredibly opaque behaviour of USB hubs.

comments.author: throw0101d
comments.text: Meta: > Somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet. I'm not going to complain against more bandwidth (as a GenXer I stared my online journey at (IIRC) 9600bps (maybe lower): much celebration with V.32/V.90), but I'm curious to know how many residential use-cases can take advantage of that much bandwidth. Linux ISOs? How many services allow that much speed on a single stream / (TCP) session? Maybe you could have five at 500 Mbps? Certainly downloading security updates or games may be quicker, but I would think that above 500Mbps (and certainly 1 Gbps) there would be major diminishing returns. Is anyone regularly getting close to that utilization in their daily work / hobbies (and not just a momentary spike on patch Tuesday)?

comments.author: nagisa
comments.text: I recently had this same problem with a multigig copper SFP+ module. These SFP+ modules (usually) advertise 10Gbps to the NIC they're plugged in, but will negotiate lower speeds on the copper side. So when NIC tries to send to SFP+ at higher rate than whatever speed SFP+ has negotiated internally, the SFP+ module will just drop a bunch of packets and incur a significant hit in throughput. These tend to not support sending pause frames to its SFP+ side either, so the best option I found was to set bandwidth limit on the NIC…

comments.author: raincole
comments.text: C# already provides many tools for your performance-critical code though. You can use pointers in unsafe. You can allocate unmanaged memory with Marshal. You can avoid copy with Span. You can even manually vectorise with Vector.IsHardwareAccelerated and such. You can also distribute apps without .NET runtime with NativeAOT. I'm sure there are people who want a C# without GC, but for me it's just... sufficient enough.

comments.author: bob1029
comments.text: The GC is a feature. Not a bug to be eliminated. GC is not surrendering control. That seems to be HN's #1 bug bear. The sensation that someone or something is taking control away from you. The proper way to frame this is that you can actually focus on the original problem you set out to solve. Risking memory leaks is crazy when it's not something the customer is demanding. Even in gaming I think the GC is fine. There are ways to spread the impact across frames and bound the amount of time spent collecting. If your clever scheme wouldn't work with a GC-managed heap, it probably won't work with one managed by hand either.

So my question is just... why?

comments.author: hedgehog
comments.text: Seems pretty promising in a few quick coding tests. 27 tokens/s decode on Ryzen 395 and llama.cpp Vulkan. Besides the obvious unmerged PRs (32694, 32657, 32429, 32704) you'll want below tiny patch for about 30% speed boost. Also, if anyone from the team is reading, if you have access for researchers I'd be interested in doing some higher volume tests & harness tuning than I have hardware for personally. --- a/src/llama-graph.cpp +++ b/src/llama-graph.cpp @@ -2670,10 +2670,12 @@ ggml_tensor \* llm_graph_context::build_moe_ffn( const float beta = hparams.situ_beta; const float lb = hparams.situ_linear_beta; - ggml_tensor \* act = ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_tanh(ctx0, ggml_scale(ctx0, cur, 1.0f/beta)), beta); + // gate/up are strided views of the fused gate_up output; ggml-vulkan's SCALE + // needs a contiguous src, so without the cont both scales fall back to the CPU + ggml_tensor \* act = ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_tanh(ctx0, ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_cont(ctx0, cur), 1.0f/beta)), beta); act = ggml_mul(ctx0, act, ggml_sigmoid(ctx0, cur)); if (lb > 0.0f) { - up = ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_tanh(ctx0, ggml_scale(ctx0, up, 1.0f/lb)), lb); + up = ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_tanh(ctx0, ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_cont(ctx0, up), 1.0f/lb)), lb); } cur = ggml_mul(ctx0, act, up); cb(cur, "ffn_moe_situ", il);

I got 2 job offers. One was through a manager from 8 years prior who was working at a place. One was a recruiter who found me on LinkedIn. I got engagement when someone physically actually knew me, they were actually hiring, and my skills overlapped. My honest advice is to apply places and try that dance, get yourself in front of people, real people, and mainly 1-1. Work everyone you have ever worked with. If you’ve reviewed their PR, they need to know that you need a job. Be kind and genuinely catch up with them if you want to, but they are your PRIMARY resource to get a job and you can’t let shame get in your way. Corporations in general are BROKEN right now in massive ways and the industry is going through a crisis. It will likely become better but whatever you have to do to survive do it. Finally, it seems like solutions architects seem in demand lately, anyone who can help customers with solutions - SWEs can tend to do well if you have some people skills.

comments.author: TacticalCoder
comments.text: Deterministic testing is one thing and it's badly needed. But I'm totally convinced we're moving to deterministic execution : n various implementations, in different languages, running on different stacks, and a minimal (maybe even hardware) voter taking care of the n-modular redundancy to pick the correct "answer". 0-day Postgres CVE? No problem: one of the implementation gives bogus answers and is detected as broken. 0-day Java? Same thing. This shall make 0-day in anything but the voters a thing of the past (and the voters shall be minimal and have a tiny attack surface). The answer can be an API query but we can go much lower: network packets, deterministically created, by n systems and all going to the voter(s). Whatever the "answer" is, it's going to be deterministic and verified from the lowest possible level. The implementations shall be written from specs, formally verified, etc. But the one thing that'll guarantee any fuck up is caught is going to be n independant implementations of the same specs. And as soon as one of the implementation/stack return even just one network packet that doesn't match what the other systems do produce: something is fucked up and has to be fixed. This shall require throwing a huge lot of the non-deterministic bullshit away but we'll see systems doing just that: n-modular redundancy and voters, at the lowest level possible. I'm 100% sure we're going there (and AI is going to write most of that for us).

comments.author: bikeshaving
comments.text: I’ve found that the “job” of using AI is mainly foible management. What the author describes here is a habit of coding agents to excessively use and create logging infrastructure, and sloppily leave it in production code even when unnecessary. For instance, I created an IPA IME keyboard ( https://ipabet.org/ ), and I found in review that Claude would leave the debugging tooling around unflagged, which essentially made the program a key-logger. These foibles come and go: early Claude Code refused to let programs crash, mangled all the comments in your codebase, and then one week you find that it insists on ending all functions with `Of` as in `layoutOf()`, `viewOf()`. Finding and mitigating these annoying habits becomes part of the job. Code review becomes articulating with this entity why certain patterns in the code are silly and should be changed. The author mentions performance and security issues as the domain of “the architect.” For performance, I’ve found that Claude Code has more or less solved this domain, and can profile and optimize code across a variety of stacks and languages using sophisticated, ad-hoc workflows. For security, it’s just an ever-ending nightmare where random habits and sloppy implementation create random vulernabilities, compounded by the fact that Anthropic has added “safeguard filters” whenever you naively say you’re looking for them. Nevertheless, I’m not sure the architecting role as they describe won’t be automated in the near future.

comments.author: rossy
comments.text: Like the weight space stuff, I think there's a small misdirection in how this is presented: Phrases like "write directly in machine code" seem to imply that ordinary LLMs intuitively understand machine code as just another language, like English or JavaScript, that they read from context and write directly as tokens, and that this intuitive understanding could mean increased efficiency or capabilities if you ask the LLM to just use the bytes rather than asking it to use the tools that human reverse engineers use. If that's what you assumed, the DeepSeek reasoning trace shatters that illusion. It's just disassembling by hand like what a human reverse engineer would do if you (sadistically?) denied them a disassembler. Yeah, the human reverse engineer would need an excellent memory of the x86_64 instruction reference, but we already know LLMs can recall a breadth of information. What we don't know, that this article also provides no evidence for, is if there will be any benefit in using the LLM for this over objdump. The article seems to intentionally conflate disassembly (computationally cheap) with decompilation (can be computationally expensive) to imply that there's some benefit to asking the LLM to work with machine code (seems impressive to the RE layman) rather than working in assembly (something you probably already assumed LLMs can do,) but the DeepSeek trace has a disassembly in it, and it's hard to imagine that inference will ever be cheaper or more reliable per-token than objdump is at producing the same output.

In its own forecast for the story, the project drags on for nine years, all the way to 2035, and still never cracks it. Just yesterday, on Friday, I was still telling students: “Maybe there is some physical law that limits how much intelligence one can get from current LLM architectures. Surely nothing in this universe is infinite.” Maybe I am right. It is just that on November 21, 2026, we have not yet reached that limit. It was 7 a.m. I opened the curtains in my study. The sun was rising. It was a sunny day. Nothing had changed. Everything had changed. Seeking some solace, I listened to a recent episode of the 3Blue1Brown podcast with host Grant Sanderson and guest Steven Strogatz (a mathematician at Cornell University who has done a lot to popularize mathematics). The two of them did have some hope that mathematics and the profession of mathematician would continue in some changed form, but they could not be sure at all. Later in the afternoon, I saw that Scott Aaronson, a theoretical computer scientist at the University of Texas at Austin, had published a blog post about the news. It ends with the following story: It was only a couple days ago that my wife and I had the following conversation: Dana: I turned off the irrigation, yet somehow water in our house is still leaking. We need to… Me: Look, a lot of the smartest people I know now think that recursive self-improvement and the end of the entire known world are coming in 12-18 months.
